title: DR Congo's Ebola Death Toll Passes 1,500 as Outbreak Becomes Second-Largest on Record
excerpt: With 3,532 confirmed cases and 1,556 deaths in less than three months, the DRC's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak now trails only the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic in scale.
body:
• The DRC's Ebola outbreak has killed 1,556 people out of 3,532 confirmed cases in under three months, making it the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record.
  • The rare Bundibugyo strain driving the outbreak has no approved vaccine or treatment, though clinical trials for two therapies began in early July.
  • Africa CDC estimates $1.4 billion is needed to contain the epidemic, but only $213.9 million has been secured so far.
  • A U.S. travel ban is restricting the flow of aid workers into the DRC, forcing organisations like Samaritan's Purse to scale back operations.

Fastest-Spreading Ebola Epidemic in History

The Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak is now the world's second-largest on record, government data released on Friday showed, with 3,532 confirmed cases and 1,556 deaths since the epidemic was declared on May 15.

Only the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak — which recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone — was larger, according to the World Health Organization.

"It's the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic that we have ever seen. The world needs to pay much more attention."

— Carl Skau, Acting Head, U.N. World Food Programme

The disease has killed five times as many people as previous outbreaks had at the same stage, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The WHO has warned the true scale could be up to four times higher than official figures suggest.

A Rare Strain With No Vaccine

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, a rare variant for which no approved vaccine or treatment exists. The more common Zaire strain, responsible for most of Congo's 16 previous Ebola outbreaks, has an approved vaccine — but it offers no protection against Bundibugyo.

Clinical trials launched on July 2 are evaluating two therapies: MBP134, a monoclonal antibody, and the antiviral remdesivir, administered alone or in combination. More than 1,200 treatment doses are currently available, according to the WHO.

Overwhelmed Response, Exhausted Workers

Ituri province in eastern Congo remains the epicentre of the outbreak. The region has been plagued by armed conflict for over 30 years, with more than 900,000 people living in displacement camps. Dozens of armed groups operate across the area, complicating humanitarian access.

Treatment centres are operating at "saturation point," WHO representative Dr. Anne Ancia said earlier this month. Patients often wait at home for beds to free up, risking further transmission. Frontline health workers went on strike in early July over unpaid wages and poor conditions, briefly walking off Ebola wards and burning tyres in front of health centres.

"The disease has now settled in the community. People continue to seek treatment from traditional healers, and the chain of transmission continues."

— Angele Gapio, Head of Emergencies, Caritas, Bunia

The epidemic has also spread beyond Ituri to the provinces of Tshopo and Haut-Uele. Four deaths have been confirmed in Kisangani, Tshopo's capital and a major trading centre of over one million people with direct links to Kinshasa.

Funding Gap and Aid Restrictions

Africa CDC said in June it would need $1.4 billion to contain the outbreak — triple its earlier estimate. Congo's May-August response plan has secured just $213.9 million of a planned $242.4 million, figures from Africa CDC and the WHO showed this week.

A U.S. travel ban is further straining the response. The Trump administration said earlier this month it was blocking American citizens in Congo from travelling to the U.S. on commercial flights. Samaritan's Purse, which runs treatment centres and relies on U.S. responders, said it would have to scale back operations because of the quarantine order.

Doctors Without Borders (MSF) warned this week that the response cannot keep pace with transmission. "We cannot continue responding to the epidemic with the same limited resources while it continues to outpace us," said Trish Newport, MSF emergency programme manager.

Global Health Implications

The outbreak carries implications well beyond central Africa. India, which maintains extensive development partnerships across the continent and plays a significant role in global health through the WHO, faces growing calls to contribute to the response. Indian pharmaceutical companies, with established capacity in antiviral and vaccine manufacturing, could potentially accelerate production of treatments if clinical trials succeed.

For the Indian diaspora in East and Central Africa, the expanding epidemic underscores the need for heightened vigilance. Several nations have issued travel advisories for the DRC, and the WHO continues to assess whether the outbreak warrants declaration as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.

With the epidemic showing no sign of slowing, aid agencies say the window to prevent a catastrophic escalation is narrowing fast.
nri_angle: India, a major contributor to global health through WHO and African development partnerships, faces pressure to scale up support as the DRC Ebola crisis deepens; Indian pharmaceutical firms could also play a role in accelerating treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain.
